prize_parts.citation: for empirical evidence on how exposure to import competition reshapes local labour markets, employment and wages, and on the persistence of adjustment costs

statement.case_for: My preferred part is still B036 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and my credited names are unchanged. I changed the citation and my alternatives, and the reasons follow. The China-shock programme gave transparent local-labour-market evidence that adjustment to trade exposure is slow, concentrated and persistent. That overturned a prior that workers and regions reallocate quickly, and the design has become a template well beyond trade. The core papers are over a decade old, so critique and refinement are already part of the record: work on shift-share identification, exposure measurement, persistence and the role of automation has qualified the magnitudes without reversing the sign of the central finding. Attribution is tighter than for any other configuration I have seen argued in this exchange. The empirical programme is jointly authored by the three names, and no supporter now proposes a fourth. Two changes follow from the chair's questions. First, I narrow the citation to exposure to import competition, local adjustment and persistence. I drop the wider phrase 'technological change' that I used in round 1. That phrase invites the task-framework and Acemoglu overlap, and a citation about trade exposure and adjustment can be defended without a ruling on the origins of the task framework. Second, the citation names no effect size. Persistence is part of the finding, so it stays in the wording. The chair summary notes that most of the convergence on B036 came from members revising during round 1, and that seven supporters is a count of stated positions, not evidence of merit. I have therefore re-tested my own case against the strongest objections, those of Friberg and Enflo on maturity and magnitudes, and I still find it holds. I also replace B010 with B034 as an alternative. The B010 credit is incomplete without Rogerson, and I do not want my own alternative to lean on a candidate where a colleague has disclosed a collaboration with a credited person.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged. The long-run magnitude and persistence of the effects, and the shift-share identification behind them, are still contested. A decade of replication shows that the central local finding survives in qualified form, but it does not settle the aggregate or long-run size. A trade-shock citation also leaves Katz and the task and skill-bias lineage uncredited. Part of that lineage involves Acemoglu (2024) and Levy and Murnane, who are outside the credited set. It also sits near the 2023 labour prize. The ballot entry bundles the two strands, so a narrow citation may look smaller than the achievement as listed, and a reasonable member could say the Committee should wait for a cleaner single discovery. There is also thematic proximity to the 2021 labour prize and to the 2024 and 2025 prizes on technology, institutions and growth. B034 has a cleaner credit structure and no comparable dispute about magnitudes. Its open questions are the 2008 overlap and the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority question. I judge B036 stronger on evidentiary transparency and on the combination of impact and credit. I do not think that judgment is beyond reasonable disagreement.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B036 only seventh because the trade and technology strands have different originators and the magnitude and persistence debate is unresolved. He would not oppose it, and says it is not clearly stronger than B020 once those disputes are weighed.
responses.response: I accept the bundling point and have acted on it by narrowing my citation to import-competition exposure and local adjustment. I do not accept that the magnitude debate is a maturity problem. The question for maturity is whether the central empirical finding has been tested hard enough to be called established, and the critiques have refined its size and its instruments without removing it. On B020, I agree that structural demand estimation is mature and widely used. But the credit question you raise, demand estimation versus Bresnahan, Reiss or the dynamic-games strand, is harder for the Committee to settle than the Dorn-versus-Katz question, which the B036 supporters resolved in round 1. Your point that structural methods answer counterfactual questions that design-based work cannot is fair. It is a reason to value both kinds of work, not a ranking of the two.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B034 and reads the B036 record as more mixed than 'held up', because exposure measures, persistence and the role of automation remain debated and the task framework overlaps with the 2024 prize. She says B034 has no comparable dispute about magnitudes.
responses.response: The B036 record is mixed on magnitudes and persistence, and my citation now says so by naming persistence and avoiding any effect size. I draw a line between a contested size and a contested discovery. The finding that import exposure lowered local employment and wages, and that adjustment was slow, is what the later work refined and did not overturn. The task-framework overlap with 2024 is the part I have stopped relying on, since I removed technology from the wording. Your point about B034 is a fair comparison. I now list it as my first alternative. Its weaknesses are different from B036's. They are the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority question and the dependence of welfare claims on model structure. I cannot resolve those from the supplied evidence. If the Committee could show that selection and reallocation is separable from both the 2008 prize and the empirical precursors, I would regard B034 as a close competitor. Your two-name credit is also cleaner than any three-name cut on B018.

responses.point: Krusell keeps B018 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford as his preferred part. He argues that the 2021-23 inflation and heterogeneous-agent work test and extend the framework without displacing it. He treats B036 as a close alternative and says the trade-shock core is better supported than a combined entry.
responses.response: I agree that post-2008 and post-2021 experience test the New Keynesian framework without removing it, and I do not hold the post-crisis record against B018 as such. My difficulty is still credit. Whether the third name is Taylor or Gali is unresolved. Even if Taylor is chosen, a trio omits Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, whose Phillips-curve and estimated-DSGE work made the framework operational. A trio there is harder to defend as the discovery than the Autor-Dorn-Hanson trio is for the China-shock programme, which the three jointly authored. You also say B036 overlaps with the 2024 prize. I have addressed that by anchoring the citation on trade-exposure evidence. I will say what would change my view. If the Committee could agree on a founding-contribution citation for B018 that names its three people without an arbitrary cut, I would give it much more weight. I have not seen that wording in the exchange so far.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers B034, says the priority concern involving Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum is his most serious reservation, and says he would now propose Autor, Dorn and Hanson if B036 were preferred. He still keeps B034 ahead because of its cleaner credit and because the trade-shock literature is still debating magnitudes.
responses.response: That is useful, because it shows the B036 attribution is not in dispute even among members who prefer another part. Your reading that Melitz supplied the tractable general-equilibrium model organising the earlier exporter facts is a reasonable way to frame B034 credit, and it would let a two-name citation avoid claiming the empirical facts. We disagree on weight. You count the magnitude debate against B036 more heavily than I do, because I take the persistence of local adjustment costs to be the finding and the magnitude to be a refinement. I would still like the Committee to review the 2008 and priority questions before a B034 vote, as I would ask it to review the shift-share critiques before a B036 vote. I would not call the two cases equally open, but I accept that the difference is a matter of judgment. If the priority question for B034 were answered, my preference between the two would be harder to state.

responses.point: Andersson moved from B018 to B036 on attribution grounds, and argues the citation should be worded around exposure and adjustment evidence, with no precise effect size claimed. He accepts that Katz and the task lineage go unrecognised and keeps B018 as an alternative.
responses.response: I agree with the wording principle and have followed it. My citation names exposure, local adjustment and persistence and does not state a magnitude. I would qualify your claim that Autor spans both strands and that this gives the citation a coherent centre. That is true, and it is why Autor's name is secure, but it does not justify crediting the whole task framework. Your own attribution reasoning, which led you to move away from B018, supports a narrow citation. I would resist adding 'technological change' to the wording. If the Committee wants it for breadth, it should be in an explicit statement of scope that says the citation is not a ruling on the origins of the task framework. Fredriksson made the same point in round 1.

uncertainties: Whether continuing critique of the shift-share exposure measures and instruments, and the long-run persistence evidence, would change the maturity judgment. A specific finding that the local-adjustment result is not robust across designs and countries would move me.

Whether leaving out Katz and the task and skill-bias lineage, including originators outside the credited set (Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane), is an acceptable attribution cost for a prize on a bundled ballot entry.

Whether the 2021 labour prize and the 2024 and 2025 prizes on technology, institutions and growth leave room for another award on the labour-market effects of trade, and whether the narrower trade-only citation reduces that concern or makes the prize look too small.
Whether B034 would be the better choice if the Committee judged the heterogeneous-firm selection mechanism separable from the 2008 prize and from the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum precursors.
Much of the convergence on B036 came from members revising their positions in round 1. I treat it as something to test and not as support for the merits.
My assessment rests on my own reading of the literature and on the supplied round-1 files, with no independent verification of credit or priority claims.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Autor, Dorn or Hanson, or to the alternatives B034 (Helpman, Melitz, Redding) and B047 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley), is apparent from my profile. I disclose the following without adjudicating them. I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell, the secretary, and of Conny Olovsson, and I have co-authored with committee colleagues Timo Boppart and Richard Friberg. I am an IIES colleague of Krusell and Boppart. Boppart discloses a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow (B010), and my round-1 alternative B010 has been dropped partly for that reason and because of the credit gap. My own research field is macroeconomics, covering climate-economy models, dynamic public finance, political economy and social mobility. I gave the 2018 presentation speech on a growth and climate-economics prize, and as chair I gave the 2025 press-release quote on a growth prize. The 2018 background cites my own work. Both prizes are thematically adjacent to the technology-and-growth overlap I discuss for B036. As chair I wrote the round-1 summary, and I am also one of the seven members counted as supporting B036. I have tried not to treat that count as merit evidence.
